title: Choosing Compute, Storage, and Network Building Blocks
bodyMarkdown:
## Compute: pick the most managed service that meets the requirement

The Well-Architected [system design principles](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/system-design) tell you to simplify and use managed services, and to prefer stateless designs. Applied to compute: start at the top of the table and move down only when a concrete requirement forces you to.

| Service | Choose when | Avoid when |
|---------|-------------|------------|
| **Cloud Run** (services, jobs, worker pools) | Stateless containers, HTTP APIs and microservices, run-to-completion jobs, pull-based background workers; scale to zero; pay for use | You need Kubernetes-level control of Pod placement, privileged workloads or cluster configuration |
| **Cloud Run functions** | Small event-driven code that glues services together | A long-lived, multi-component service |
| **GKE Autopilot** | Kubernetes API and ecosystem needed, Google manages nodes and scaling; Google's recommended default mode for most GKE workloads | Workloads that need privileges or configuration Autopilot does not allow |
| **GKE Standard** | Granular control over cluster settings, node pools, Pod placement, special privileges | You do not need that control (you take on node operations for nothing) |
| **Compute Engine (MIGs)** | Lift-and-shift, custom OS or kernel, licensing tied to VMs, special hardware, full control | You want zero infrastructure operations |

[Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run) offers services (HTTP behind a unique HTTPS endpoint, autoscaled), jobs (run to completion) and worker pools (continuous pull-based work such as Pub/Sub or Kafka consumers, scaled manually). Idle services scale to zero, and billing is request-based (no idle charge) or instance-based.

The GKE [mode guidance](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/choose-cluster-mode) is explicit: use Autopilot for most workloads unless your application needs privileges or configuration that Autopilot constraints do not allow. In Autopilot, GKE manages the cluster infrastructure including nodes and scaling; in Standard you configure node pools and scaling yourself.

Exam heuristic: dozens of interdependent services with a service mesh, GPU inference and fine-grained scheduling is GKE; a single new stateless container that must scale to zero is Cloud Run. A single large VM running Docker Compose is never the answer for a platform that needs orchestration.

### Machine families and custom machine types

Per the [machine families guide](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/machine-resource), choose the family by workload shape before you size anything.

| Family | Example series | Choose for |
|--------|---------------|-----------|
| **General-purpose** | N4, N2, E2, N1 | Web servers, microservices, databases, dev and test |
| **Compute-optimized** | C4, C3, H3, C2 | HPC, EDA, scientific and other compute-bound work |
| **Memory-optimized** | M4, M3, X4 | SAP HANA and in-memory stores; up to 12 TB of memory |
| **Storage-optimized** | Z3 | Highest block-storage-to-compute ratio: scan-heavy databases and search |
| **Accelerator-optimized** | A3, A4, G2 | GPU workloads: ML training and inference, CUDA-based HPC |

**Custom machine types** exist only in some general-purpose series (N4, N4D, N4A, N2, N2D, E2, N1) and the G2 GPU series, per the [custom machine type guide](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/creating-instance-with-custom-machine-type). They allow 2 to 8 GB of memory per vCPU in 256 MiB steps, with vCPU counts that follow series rules (N2 and N4: even numbers up to 80). Extended memory above that ratio is available on most of these series but does not qualify for resource-based committed use discounts. Custom types carry roughly a 5% premium over predefined. Choose one when no predefined shape fits, for example a memory-heavy but CPU-light service, or when per-vCPU software licensing makes every unused vCPU a cost. Do not reach for custom when a compute-optimized, memory-optimized or accelerator-optimized family is what the workload actually needs: those families have no custom shapes.

### Compute cost levers

- **Spot VMs.** Discounts of up to 91% for many machine types, GPUs, TPUs and Local SSDs, per the [Spot VM documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/spot). Spot VMs have no minimum or maximum runtime unless you set one, are not guaranteed to be available, and are excluded from the Compute Engine SLA. The preemption notice defaults to 0 seconds and can be configured up to 120 seconds. Use for fault-tolerant, checkpointed batch work.
- **Committed use discounts.** Per the [CUD overview](https://cloud.google.com/docs/cuds), resource-based CUDs cover Compute Engine resources in a region, while spend-based CUDs cover a minimum dollar commitment (compute flexible commitments span Compute Engine, GKE and Cloud Run). Terms are one or three years and the commitment is billed monthly whether or not you use it, so commit only to the steady baseline.
- **Right-sizing.** Compute Engine [machine type recommendations](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/apply-machine-type-recommendations-for-instances) use the previous 8 days of metrics, can suggest a custom type, and are not available for memory-optimized families or GPU and TPU instances.
- **Scale to zero when idle.** Cloud Run does it natively. Per the [autoscaler documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/autoscaler), a MIG reaches zero only with schedule-based autoscaling and `minNumReplicas` set to 0, not on CPU, load balancing or monitoring-metric signals.

## Storage: match the data shape and access pattern

| Need | Service | Key point |
|------|---------|-----------|
| Objects, media, backups, data lake | **Cloud Storage** | Unlimited storage, four cold-to-hot classes, lifecycle rules |
| Shared POSIX file system over NFS | **Filestore** | Mountable by many VMs and GKE concurrently |
| Block storage for a VM | **Persistent Disk** | Attached to VMs; snapshots for backup |
| Relational, regional, MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQL Server | **Cloud SQL** | Fully managed; HA is zonal |
| Relational, global scale, strong consistency | **Spanner** | Horizontal scale with SQL and ACID transactions |
| Wide-column NoSQL, huge throughput, time series | **Bigtable** | No SQL joins or multi-row transactions |
| Document store for mobile and web apps | **Firestore** | Serverless, real-time sync, transactions |
| Analytics warehouse | **BigQuery** | Analytical queries rather than OLTP |

[Spanner](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/) multi-region configurations (99.999% SLA, replicas across regions) fit a globally distributed inventory that needs strongly consistent writes. [Cloud SQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/introduction) suits regional relational workloads and lift-and-shift of MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server, but its HA does not span regions. [Bigtable](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/overview) scales to billions of rows for time-series and IoT. [Firestore](https://cloud.google.com/firestore) is serverless with mobile and web SDKs.

### Cloud Storage classes

The [storage classes](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/storage-classes) differ in price structure and minimum storage duration, not in access latency: every class serves data with millisecond latency, including Archive.

| Class | Intended access | Minimum storage duration | Notes |
|-------|----------------|--------------------------|-------|
| **Standard** | Frequent | None | 99.9% regional SLA, 99.95% multi-region |
| **Nearline** | About once a month or less | 30 days | Retrieval fees; 99.0% regional SLA |
| **Coldline** | About once a quarter or less | 90 days | Higher retrieval cost than Nearline |
| **Archive** | Long-term archive, rarely read | 365 days | Lowest storage price; data still available within milliseconds |

Rapid Storage, a newer zonal-bucket class, is performance-oriented rather than a cold tier. For seven-year audit logs read about once a year, Archive minimizes cost.

Use [Object Lifecycle Management](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle) to automate this. Actions are Delete, SetStorageClass (only to equal or colder classes, for example Standard to Nearline to Coldline to Archive) and AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload. Conditions include age, createdBefore, numNewerVersions, prefix and suffix matches and size; all conditions in a rule must match. Actions run asynchronously, and configuration changes can take up to 24 hours to apply.

### Filestore

[Filestore tiers](https://cloud.google.com/filestore/docs/service-tiers) are Zonal (1 TiB to 100 TiB, aimed at HPC and localized workloads), Regional (100 GiB to 100 TiB, for regional resilience) and Enterprise with multishares for GKE (1 TiB to 10 TiB). They support NFSv3 and NFSv4.1 with backups and snapshots.

## Network: connectivity, privacy and load balancing

**VPC fundamentals.** Per the [VPC documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc), a VPC network and its routes and firewall rules are global, while subnets are regional. New projects get a default auto mode network with one subnet per region from 10.128.0.0/9. Custom mode, where you create subnets and ranges yourself, is the recommended choice for production, and the conversion from auto to custom is one-way. Plan CIDRs across VPCs and on-premises before connecting anything.

**Firewalls.** Per the [firewall documentation](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewalls), VPC firewall rules are stateful and have an implied allow-all egress and deny-all ingress. Priority runs from 0 to 65,535 (default 1000, lowest number wins), and targets are all instances, network tags or service accounts, never a mix of tags and service accounts. For guardrails across many VPCs, use hierarchical firewall policies at the organization or folder, or network firewall policies (Cloud NGFW) with secure tags. Cloud NGFW tiers add FQDN filtering, geolocation and threat intelligence (Standard) or TLS inspection, URL filtering and an intrusion prevention system (Enterprise). Per-application ports belong in VPC rules; organization-wide denies belong in policies.

**Container networking.** [VPC-native GKE clusters](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/alias-ips) use alias IPs: nodes take the subnet's primary range, and Pods and Services take secondary ranges, so Pod IPs are routable in the VPC and work with peering and NEGs. VPC-native is the default for new clusters; legacy routes-based clusters lack NEG support. Autopilot allows up to 32 Pods per node, and Standard is configurable up to 110. Exhausting the Pod range blocks scale-out, so size it for growth. [GKE Dataplane V2](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/dataplane-v2) is the eBPF-based (Cilium) dataplane with built-in NetworkPolicy enforcement, default on new Autopilot clusters and available only on new clusters.

**Private connectivity options.**

| Option | What it does | IP overlap | Transitive |
|--------|-------------|------------|-----------|
| **[VPC Network Peering](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc-peering)** | Exchanges routes between two VPCs | Not allowed: no subnet range may match, contain or fit within a peer's range | No |
| **[Private Service Connect](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/private-service-connect)** | Consumer reaches a producer service through an internal IP endpoint in its own VPC | Allowed: NAT removes any IP coordination between consumer and producer | Not applicable |
| **[Cloud NAT](https://cloud.google.com/nat/docs/overview)** | Outbound translation so VMs, GKE, Cloud Run and App Engine standard need no external IPs | n/a | n/a |

Private Service Connect reaches Google APIs such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery and published services through service attachments. Cloud NAT is regional and allows no unsolicited inbound connections, so it cannot expose a service.

**Hybrid connectivity.** HA VPN (IPsec over the internet), Dedicated Interconnect, Partner Interconnect and Cross-Cloud Interconnect; capacities and selection are in Module 4.

**Load balancing.** From the [load balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/load-balancing-overview): global external Application Load Balancers use a single anycast IP with multi-region backends; regional external ones are single-region and available in both Network Service Tiers; internal Application Load Balancers are reachable only inside the VPC (regional or cross-region). Network Load Balancers work at layer 4, either proxy-based or passthrough; passthrough preserves client source IPs with direct server return. Premium Tier uses Google's global backbone and supports global load balancers; Standard Tier is regional, trading performance for cost.

## Decision approach

Extract the NFRs first, then choose storage from data shape (the hardest decision to reverse), the most managed compute that fits, networking, and cost levers last.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **GKE by default.** Running a single simple stateless service on a cluster adds node and upgrade operations for no benefit.
- **Cloud Run for everything,** including workloads needing privileged containers or Kubernetes primitives.
- **Spot for stateful or deadline-bound work** with no checkpointing; Spot VMs carry no SLA.
- **CUDs sized to peak.** You pay for the commitment whether or not you use it.
- **Cloud Storage as a shared POSIX file system.** Use Filestore when applications need file semantics.
- **Bigtable for relational needs** or Cloud SQL for global write scale.
- **Nearline or Coldline for data read often,** where retrieval fees and minimum durations erase the savings.
- **Peering with overlapping ranges,** or expecting peering to be transitive; **Cloud NAT as an ingress path**; **auto mode networks in production**.
- **A custom machine type for a workload that needs a specialized family,** or a Pod range too small for the cluster's growth.

## Exam tips

- **Most managed that fits.** New stateless container, scale to zero, no node management: Cloud Run. Many interdependent services needing mesh, custom networking and GPU scheduling: GKE.
- **Autopilot is the default GKE recommendation;** pick Standard only for privileges or configuration Autopilot does not allow.
- **Shared POSIX across VMs and GKE is Filestore;** Persistent Disk is block storage for a VM and Cloud Storage is object storage.
- **Global, strongly consistent, relational with horizontal write scale is Spanner.** Bigtable is for key-based wide-column throughput without joins; Cloud SQL is regional relational.
- **Cold classes are about price and minimum duration, not retrieval speed.** Rarely read, kept for years: Archive, plus a lifecycle rule to move data there.
- **Private Service Connect when ranges overlap or must not be coordinated;** VPC Peering needs non-overlapping, non-transitive connections.
- **Pick the family by workload shape.** Memory-optimized for SAP HANA and in-memory stores, compute-optimized for HPC, accelerator-optimized for GPUs; custom machine types exist only in some general-purpose series and G2, so they never replace those families.
- **GKE needs VPC-native networking planned up front.** Pod and Service ranges are secondary subnet ranges; size them for growth, and enforce NetworkPolicy with Dataplane V2.
- **Spot for fault-tolerant batch, CUDs for the steady baseline,** never CUDs for peak capacity and never Spot for work that cannot be interrupted.
- **Single anycast IP and nearest-healthy-region routing means a global external Application Load Balancer** (add Cloud CDN for cacheable content).
